stories.headline: Week 11 winners and losers: Cowboys put up points while Josh Allen does not
stories.summary: Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb and Jonah Coleman put fantasy teams on their backs in Week 11, while Josh Allen, Jonathan Taylor and Tony Pollard disappointed.
stories.byline: Matt Bowen and Tristan H. Cockcroft
stories.body:
The Dallas Cowboys and Kansas City Chiefs both had outstanding fantasy performances from their stars, as Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce put up plenty of points in their respective matchups. But stars such as Josh Allen, Jonathan Taylor and Tony Pollard all had less-than-stellar outings that surely disappointed their fantasy managers.

The fantasy playoffs are just around the corner with some key matchups still to play beyond Week 11. So, who were the big winners and losers around the league? Matt Bowen and Tristan H. Cockcroft offer their analysis.

Jump to a topic:

Ranking winners | Ranking losers

Biggest injuries and what's next

Ranking fantasy winners of Week 11
1. The Cowboys' offense
In a positive matchup versus the subpar Titans defense, this Cowboys offense dropped 50 points -- and their playmakers showed up. Prescott had a season-high 35.9 points as he threw for 325 yards and four touchdowns, plus he added another score on a low red zone scramble. Lamb scored 30.2 points (his second game of 30 or more in his past three), as he caught 11 of 12 targets for 132 yards and a touchdown, while George Pickens (23.8 points) brought in seven of 10 targets for 102 yards and a touchdown. And let's not forget about running back Javonte Williams, as he had 91 total yards -- on 18 touches -- with two touchdowns (24.1 points). Next up, Dallas gets a tougher test versus the Eagles' defense in the afternoon game on Thanksgiving Day. -- Bowen

2. Jonah Coleman, RB, Denver Broncos
Coleman's 34.9 points versus the Raiders were a career high and the second most of any player through the late window. Coleman had 111 yards rushing and three touchdowns on 24 carries, and he finished with four receptions for 18 yards. With three straight games of 18 or more points (and at least 15 touches), it's clear that Coleman is the lead back in Denver. With a Week 12 matchup versus Pittsburgh, managers can play Coleman as a midtier RB1. -- Bowen

3. Patrick Mahomes, QB, and Travis Kelce, TE, Kansas City Chiefs
The Chiefs' passing game kept rolling in Kansas City's second game since deepening its receiver corps with the acquisition of WR Josh Downs. Mahomes scored 24.96 fantasy points, his third game with at least that many in the past four weeks, while Kelce scored more points in the first half of the contest than he had in the entirety of any game since Week 7 of 2023, finishing his day with 25.4. The Chiefs have a pair of upcoming road games (versus the Buffalo Bills in Week 12 and the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 14) in which Mahomes will need to throw early and often -- including leaning on Kelce -- to keep up on the scoreboard. Both players are top-10 weekly positional options for the stretch run. -- Cockcroft
4. Jared Goff, QB, and Jameson Williams, WR, Detroit Lions
Goff scored 20.36 points in Sunday's win over the Bucs, his second straight game with 20 or more points. Goff threw for 279 yards and two touchdowns, plus he rushed for a season-high 12 yards on five carries. Williams scored 19.3 points, catching all four of his targets for 93 yards and a score. With a Thanksgiving matchup versus the Bears defense up next, Goff will be a lower-tier QB1 in my rankings, while Williams remains a big-play WR2/Flex. -- Bowen

5. Ashton Jeanty, RB, Las Vegas Raiders
Remarkably, Jeanty scored his second-most fantasy points in a game all season (27.9), despite totaling only 16 touches. It was testament to his big-play ability, as Jeanty had a 68-yard receiving touchdown and broke off a 46-yard run in the second quarter. He clearly outplayed Mike Washington Jr. in this game, and it's fair to question whether Jeanty might recapture his primary running back role for Week 12. Jeanty is shaping up as a high-end fantasy RB2 for that matchup against the Cleveland Browns. -- Cockcroft

6. Jahmyr Gibbs, RB, Detroit Lions
Considering the difficulty of the matchup -- the Tampa Bay Buccaneers entered the week with the No. 1 defense against running backs -- Gibbs' 27.8 fantasy points were quite impressive. He has now scored 281.2 points for the season, the seventh most in history by any running back through his team's first 10 games. Gibbs is fantasy football's best player, and he has only one remotely scary matchup left in Week 15, at the Minnesota Vikings, but he has proved himself matchup-proof. -- Cockcroft

7. Chuba Hubbard, RB, Carolina Panthers
He continued his clear fantasy RB1 campaign with his fifth game of 20-plus carries and fourth of 24-plus fantasy points in his past seven games. Unfortunately, he has his two most challenging matchups up next: against the Buccaneers in Week 12 and the Vikings in Week 13. Hubbard's usage -- he has had at least 70% numbers in terms of snap rate and rushing share in seven of 10 games -- props him up as a universal start, but we might be looking at fantasy scores in the teens for those games. -- Cockcroft

8. Emmett Johnson, RB, Kansas City Chiefs
Making his second straight start for an injured Kenneth Walker III (groin), Johnson scored 24.3 points. The rookie, who now has back-to-back games of 24 or more points, rushed for 105 yards and a touchdown on 23 carries, while he caught four passes for 38 yards. If Walker is still out for the Week 12 matchup versus the Bills, Johnson will stick as a top-five RB due to his dual-threat usage in Andy Reid's offense. -- Bowen

9. DJ Moore, WR, Buffalo Bills
He might have had his share of injuries this season, but he is quite a good fit as Josh Allen's No. 1 receiver when he's healthy. Moore's 23.1 fantasy points and 10 targets were both season bests, and he has at least 16 points in three of his past four games. For so long as he is available, he's a fantasy WR2 for a competitive stretch of upcoming games in which he'll be sorely needed (KC, @NE, @GB, CHI, @DEN). -- Cockcroft

Ranking fantasy losers of Week 11
1. Josh Allen, QB, Buffalo Bills
It's the first time Allen has gone without a rushing attempt -- excluding Week 17/18 regular-season finales in which he was rested early -- in his career. Allen had to do it all with his arm in Week 11, and two interceptions resulted in his scoring a season-low 12.16 fantasy points. It's not a performance his managers should expect to see again, especially not with a Thanksgiving night matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs -- which should be a high-scoring game -- up next. -- Cockcroft

2. Jonathan Taylor, RB, Indianapolis Colts
Taylor scored only 6.7 points in the loss to the Texans on Thursday night, as he rushed for 21 yards on 11 carries and tallied four catches for six yards. Taylor did out-touch Seth McGowan 15 to 4; however, Taylor has now scored fewer than 10 points in three of his last four games. With Anthony Richardson Sr. now taking over as the starting quarterback (after the team released Daniel Jones), Taylor could see more daylight as a runner on zone-read and misdirection backfield action. But don't count on Taylor getting a bump in the pass game here, and he should be viewed as an RB2 for the Week 12 matchup versus the Giants. -- Bowen

3. Tony Pollard, RB, Tennessee Titans
It's perhaps harsh to place him here, considering he rushed for 110 yards while averaging 5.2 yards per carry. But after his recent run of productivity in the receiving department, it's a disappointment that he had only one target -- which he failed to catch. Pollard's minimal passing-game usage was puzzling, considering his Titans trailed the Cowboys by at least 10 points for the final 46 minutes, which wasn't far off the game script from Week 10 when he scored 20.6 fantasy points receiving alone. He has a much tougher matchup in a rematch of that Week 10 game, facing the Jacksonville Jaguars next week. Pollard will be a high-end fantasy RB2 for that contest. -- Cockcroft

4. D'Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai, RBs, Chicago Bears
The Bears' backfield is truly struggling, even with Monangai back in action. Swift was held under 12 fantasy points for a second straight game and under four yards per carry for a fifth straight, while Monangai scored 1.8 points and averaged 2.3 yards per carry. Swift played 47% of the offensive snaps and had 13 carries; Monangai played 38% and ran eight times. It's difficult to get behind Swift as more than a low-end fantasy RB2, and Monangai is a matchups-oriented flex. -- Cockcroft

5. Luther Burden III, WR, Chicago Bears
After scoring 17 or more points in his previous four games, Burden had a season-low 3.3 points in Sunday's win, catching two of three targets for 10 yards and registering one carry for three yards. This Bears' passing offense lacked rhythm from the jump versus the Saints, and the poor rushing efficiency didn't help. After this ugly game, Burden will look to rebound Thursday against the Lions. -- Bowen

6. Jaylen Warren, RB, Pittsburgh Steelers
Warren had a season-low 4.9 points in Sunday's loss to the Eagles, rushing for 28 yards on nine carries and catching two passes for one yard. It was Warren's second straight game with fewer than 10 points, and Rico Dowdle's usage (nine touches) should be concerning for managers. In a Steelers offense that looks really poor right now, I'll have Warren ranked as a lower-tier RB2, with Dowdle in the flex range, for the Week 12 matchup versus the Broncos' defense. -- Bowen

7. Garrett Wilson, WR, New York Jets
His 6.9 fantasy points represented the fourth time in his past seven games that he has been held beneath 10, during which time his role has been awfully variable. Wilson has seen 11 or more targets in three of those seven games but five or fewer in three others -- he had five in Week 11 -- making him one of the position's most inconsistent players. As the Jets' No. 1 receiver, he remains a viable fantasy WR2, but his no-rhyme-or-reason results are certainly frustrating to his managers. -- Cockcroft

8. Bhayshul Tuten, RB, Jacksonville Jaguars
He scored only 8.3 fantasy points and played 43% of the Jaguars' offensive snaps, his worst and second-worst numbers all season. Tuten entered having been dealing with ankle and foot injuries, and he was on the sideline for a portion of this game too, raising concerns about whether his ailments are hindering his performance. He has totaled 53 fewer rushing yards than expected the past three weeks. Tuten's Week 12 matchup is outstanding (TEN), but it's best to temper expectations to high-end fantasy RB2 levels. -- Cockcroft

9. Trevor Lawrence, QB, Jacksonville Jaguars
Lawrence threw for 301 yards in the Jags' Week 11 loss to the Giants, but he finished with one touchdown (as compared with two interceptions), and he rushed for only seven yards (12.74 points). Pressure changes things. And we saw that Sunday, as Lawrence was forced to move in the pocket, plus he was sacked three times by the Giants' pass rush. Lawrence gets the Titans in Week 12, the same defense he scored 26.7 points on back in Week 10. With a prime matchup, Lawrence will be a top-five QB in my rankings. -- Bowen

10. Cam Skattebo, RB, New York Giants
Skattebo had 17 touches in the Giants' Week 11 win over the Jaguars, but he managed only 48 total yards, lost a fumble and finished with 5.8 points. A touchdown-dependent grinder, Skattebo gets a positive matchup against the Colts defense in Week 12, a unit that ranks in the bottom 10 versus running backs. He'll be an RB2 for me. -- Bowen

11. Jordyn Tyson, WR, New Orleans Saints
Back in Week 10, Tyson caught 11 passes for 80 yards (19.0 points), but his usage and production really declined in Sunday's loss. The rookie saw just two targets, catching one for six yards, and he added one rushing attempt for four yards (2.0 points). With Chris Olave catching 9 of 15 targets in this one, Tyson didn't get much work. I'll still have Tyson in my ranks for the Week 12 game at Cincinnati, but he'll be in the Flex range. -- Bowen

12. DK Metcalf, WR, Pittsburgh Steelers
It's hard to trust Metcalf right now. In Sunday's loss to the Eagles, Metcalf caught just one of four targets for six yards (season-low 1.2 points) before being ejected in the third quarter for his second personal foul/unsportsmanlike conduct. Metcalf has scored fewer than 10 points in three of his last four games (with fewer than two points in two of his last three), and the Denver secondary looms next week. He can't be played as more than a boom/bust WR3. -- Bowen

Injury impact

Justin Herbert, QB, Los Angeles Chargers

What we know: Following the Chargers Week 11 loss to the Jets, Herbert was placed in concussion protocol. Herbert scored a season-high 22.44 points throwing for 132 yards and two touchdowns, while rushing for 32 yards and a touchdown on eight carries.

What's next: We'll follow updates this week on Herbert, but if he is down for the Week 12 game versus the Patriots, No.2 quarterback DJ Uiagalelei would be in line to start. Stay tuned. -- Bowen

stories.headline: Adebayo gets triple-double, Heat (without Giannis) top Thunder (without SGA) for 7th straight win
stories.summary: — Bam Adebayo scored 24 points and had a triple-double, Pelle Larsson scored 21 and the shorthanded Miami Heat beat the very shorthanded Oklahoma City Thunder 123-113 on Sunday night to push their winning streak to seven games.
stories.body:
MIAMI -- — Bam Adebayo scored 24 points and had a triple-double, Pelle Larsson scored 21 and the shorthanded Miami Heat beat the very shorthanded Oklahoma City Thunder 123-113 on Sunday night to push their winning streak to seven games.


Adebayo finished with 15 rebounds and 12 assists, his ninth career triple-double in regular season play. He's also had one in the postseason.


Nikola Jović scored 15 and Davion Mitchell added 14 for Miami, which had seven players in double figures.


Bennett Stirtz scored 21 for Oklahoma City, which got 20 from Jared McCain, 17 from Ajay Mitchell and 13 from Josh Dix.


Both teams were missing past Most Valuable Players. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander — the two-time reigning MVP — was out for Oklahoma City with a neck strain and lower back contusion, while Miami was without Giannis Antetokounmpo because of a groin strain.


It was the first game missed for both Gilgeous-Alexander and Antetokounmpo this season. The Thunder, who have dealt with serious injury issues all season, had only nine available players — three of them under two-way contracts.


And the Thunder never went away, getting down by 20 early in the fourth before outscoring Miami 33-23 in the final 10:36.


Miami led wire-to-wire for the third consecutive game. It’s the first time in the NBA’s era of digitized play-by-play, starting in 1996, that the Heat went three straight games without trailing.


The Heat became the fourth team in NBA history to improve their record to 10-6 (or better) through 16 games after an 0-4 start. The others: Dallas (12-4) in 2006-07, Oklahoma City (10-6) in 2018-19 and Sacramento (10-6) in 2022-23.


Miami matched its longest win streak since a 13-game unbeaten run from Jan. 17 through Feb. 10, 2017. The Heat had three other seven-game streaks since, the most recent spanning January and February of last season.


Up next
Thunder: Visit Indiana on Monday.


Heat: Visit Philadelphia on Wednesday.


------

stories.headline: Heeney headlines returning Swans at pre-season training
stories.summary: After months of off-field turmoil in the fallout from the Pullman Hotel scandal, the Sydney Swans have welcomed back four AFL players for pre-season training.
stories.body:
High-profile Sydney Swans player Isaac Heeney has returned to training as the AFL club's embattled quartet aims to resurrect their playing careers.

Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice took part in the Swans' first-to-fourth-year pre-season training on Monday after months of off-field turmoil following the Pullman Hotel scandal.

The quartet, alongside now-North Melbourne player Nick Blakey, had served a season-ending suspension for what the club termed a "serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

Separate from the AFL-endorsed bans, Heeney, Warner, Jordon and Blakey were under investigation after three women made reports of sexual assault to Victoria Police.

Police have since confirmed the players would not be charged due to insufficient evidence.

Civil claims are still being prepared against relevant parties.

Swans forward Tom Papley was also at the club's first pre-season session after being slapped with a three-game ban by the AFL for conduct unbecoming.

The 30-year-old, one of the team's most experienced players, had returned a positive roadside test for the presence of cocaine and MDMA.

Papley had been pulled over by NSW Police for a random roadside drug test on November 2, with checks revealing his licence was suspended due to non-payment of a parking fine.

The initial roadside test returned a positive reading and a secondary sample of oral fluid was taken.

On top of his AFL ban, Papley has been fined $722 by police and his licence will be suspended for three months.

He will face Waverley Local Court for driving with a suspended licence on November 26.

Papley, who underwent post-season surgery on both knees, did not take part in Monday's main session.

He was joined by fellow forwards Logan McDonald and Hayden McLean in the rehabilitation group.

stories.headline: Tage Thompson scores twice as Sabres top Lightning, 6-2
stories.summary: — Tage Thompson scored twice, Zach Benson had a goal and two assists and Ukka-Pekka Luukkonen finished with 29 saves and the Buffalo Sabres beat the Tampa Bay Lightning 6-2 on Sunday.
stories.body:
TAMPA, Fla. -- — Tage Thompson scored twice, Zach Benson had a goal and two assists and Ukka-Pekka Luukkonen finished with 29 saves and the Buffalo Sabres beat the Tampa Bay Lightning 6-2 on Sunday.


Noah Ostlund had a goal and two points. Jack Quinn and Jiri Kulich also scored for Buffalo.


The Sabres won for the second time in the past eight games.


Nikita Kucherov and Gage Goncalves scored for Tampa Bay, which suffered only its second loss on home ice this season in 12 games (10-2-0). Dennis Hildeby finished with 22 saves to suffer his first regulation loss this season in his sixth start.


Thompson has goals in four consecutive games and 12 goals in his past 12 games. His 33rd career multi-goal game ties Pat LaFontaine for 10th most in franchise history.


Thompson's two goals 5:12 apart in the second period broke open the game for Buffalo. He scored on a one-timer from the left circle for a 5-on-3 power play goal for a 3-1 lead then danced around Pontus Holmberg, who lost his stick, to get to the middle slot for a wrist shot at 16:17.


It was the 18th multi-goal period for Thompson, tying Dave Andreychuk for fifth most in franchise history.


Quinn increased his goal-scoring streak to three games, converting a 2-on-1 chance 1:22 into the second period to break a 1-1 tie.


Goncalves notched his first of the season to bring the Lightning to within 4-2 at 5:50 of the third period, but Ostlund put Buffalo back ahead by three goals a minute later. Benson added an empty net goal with 1:09 left.


Up next
Sabres: Host New York Rangers on Wednesday


Lightning: Host Carolina on Wednesday

stories.headline: Cincinnati stuns Shield-winners Nashville to start best-of-3 series
stories.summary: Roman Celentano made six saves for his fourth clean sheet of the season as FC Cincinnati took advantage of an early own goal to earn a 1-0 victory over Nashville SC on Sunday.
stories.body:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- Roman Celentano made six saves for his fourth clean sheet of the season as FC Cincinnati took advantage of an early own goal to earn a 1-0 victory over Nashville SC on Sunday to begin a best-of-three series.

Cincinnati needs one more win to knock out the Supporters' Shield winner -- and MLS single-season points record holder -- with Game 2 scheduled for Saturday.

Nashville lost its first home match of the season after entering 15-0-2 in MLS play at GEODIS Park and outscoring opponents 48-14. Nashville is looking to become the ninth Supporters' Shield winner to win the MLS Cup in the league's 31-year history.

Cincinnati took the lead in the seventh minute. Nashville midfielder Patrick Yazbek came under pressure and tried to play it back to goalkeeper Brian Schwake, who was out of his area, but inadvertently curled into the back of his own net.

Cincinnati appeared to go ahead 2-0 in the 11th minute after a corner kick, but the glancing header was disallowed for a questionable foul in the box.

Nashville had several scoring chances in the second half. Hany Mukhtar had a shot deflect off the crossbar in the 63rd. Then, Sam Surridge appeared to score in the 75th, but Mukhtar was caught offside.

Celentano denied Mukhtar's close-range attempt in the 81st.

B.J. Callaghan's Nashville side set league records for points (77), wins (23), home wins (15), goals conceded (25), and fewest losses (three) this season. Nashville also tied the MLS record with 17 clean sheets and allowed just 25 goals, the fewest in the modern era of MLS.

Information from The Associated Press was used in this recap.

stories.headline: Haas confirm Rafa Camara will finish 2026 season with the team
stories.summary: Brazilian driver Rafa Camara will complete the 2026 season with Haas ahead of his full rookie season in 2027, the team confirmed on Sunday.
stories.body:
Brazilian driver Rafa Camara will complete the 2026 season with Haas ahead of his full rookie season in 2027, the team confirmed on Sunday.

Formula 2 championship leader Camara took the place of ousted Esteban Ocon in Brazil and continued in the seat at this week's Las Vegas Grand Prix.

He will race for the team in Qatar on Nov. 29 and Abu Dhabi on Dec. 6. The Ferrari junior had already been confirmed to be replacing Ocon in 2027, but the Frenchman's sudden sacking during the Mexico City Grand Prix accelerated his F1 debut.

Haas' decision will likely cost Camara the chance to be F2 champion. F1's main feeder series will finish its own championship four races spread across the schedule in Qatar and Abu Dhabi -- Camara holds a slender seven-point lead over Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov, with Alpine junior Alex Dunne 18 points back.

Team boss Aayo Komatsu said the opportunity for Camara to embed further into the team was too good to turn down. "We're excited to be able to finish the season with Rafa driving and build on his first two race starts with the team in Brazil and America," Komatsu said.

"I'm delighted that Rafa's embraced every track session as a learning opportunity and embedded himself further within the team. We now get to finish the season together which is advantageous to all of us ahead of a relatively short off-season and as our 2027 preparations get underway."

Haas had one other option if they had wanted Camara to finish off his F2 campaign -- reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa filled in for Ocon in Mexico City and scored a top-ten finish on his debut.

Camara will keep driving alongside fellow Ferrari junior Oliver Bearman in the final races. Although it is expected to be completed soon, Bearman has not had a new Haas deal confirmed yet.

Bearman is understood to be in talks with Ferrari about their wider plans for his career, mindful of what happens with him should Lewis Hamilton extend his stay with the team beyond 2027.

stories.headline: DiBernardo joins Rapinoe, Pulisic in pantheon of great Olimpicos
stories.summary: Vanessa DiBernardo joined an elite list on Saturday, scoring for Kansas City direct from a corner. Known in soccer circles as an Olimpico, here are some of the very best.
stories.body:
(Editor's note: This article was originally published on Oct. 2, 2025, and it has been updated after Vanessa DiBernardo's stunner in Saturday's NWSL championship finale.)

For a relatively simple sport, soccer is filled with novelties.

Outfield players don the gloves and go into goal when there's no other option, penalty takers attempt chipped "Panenka" spot kicks to varying degrees of success, goalkeepers sprint the length of the pitch to come up for last-minute corners -- and sometimes they even score. And every now and then, players will score directly from a corner kick.

Highly improbable, sometimes intentional, a goal scored in this way is known as a Gol Olimpico, an Olympic goal.

But how did these goals get their name? The history of the Olimpico is irrevocably intertwined with South American football and with one of its great rivalries: Uruguay vs. Argentina.

- New Premier League record set with eight injury-time goals

- From World Cup Willie to Ciao: Ranking every World Cup mascot

- NWSL has more money than ever, yet its biggest problems remain

On June 9, 1924, Uruguay won the Olympic gold medal in Paris after defeating Switzerland 3-0. Around the same time in June 1924, the International Football Association Board (IFAB) changed the laws around corner kicks, making goals scored directly from the corner legal. But it wasn't until Oct. 2, 1924, that these two pieces of information would combine to create the Olimpico moniker.

Following Uruguay's Olympic victory, they played a two-game friendly series with their South American neighbors Argentina. The teams played out a 1-1 draw in Montevideo in late-September before travelling to Buenos Aires.

The return match was suspended after four minutes due to the large crowd on the sideline and was rescheduled for Oct. 2. Argentina would eventually win the rematch 2-1, but the whole game was filled with controversy. La Celeste withdrew from the match with four minutes remaining and both sides accused the other of excessive aggression.

But the important part of this story happened in the 15th minute, when Argentina's Cesareo Onzari whipped in a corner and scored.

The audacity of the goal and La Albiceleste defeating the Olympic champions was the catalyst for local journalists to dub the goal an Olympic one. From then on, whenever other goals were scored in this fashion, they were described as like the one scored against the Olympians, and soon the label Gol Olimpico was applied to all such goals.

The Olimpico is stunning when it's intentional and sometimes comical when it's not. It really has no right to work considering where players are standing on the field, how much of the target they can see from that position and what they need to do to the ball to make it curve into the back of the net. Whether they dribble through at the near post or sail past everyone into the far corner, there's beauty in the curl of ball, the audacity, the incredulity. It's glorious.

Take Vanessa DiBernardo's opening goal in Saturday's NWSL championship game. The Kansas City Current were set on course for their first NWSL title thanks to DiBernardo's Olimpico in the 54th minute, with the ball curling over everyone's head to nestle into the far corner of the next.

From regular-season matches to finals, the Olympics and even the World Cup, here are some of the very best Olimpicos.

Vanessa DiBernardo, Kansas City Current vs. Washington Spirit | 2026 NWSL championship

Kansas City fans will never forget how the Current's first NWSL championship was secured thanks in large part to DiBernado's kick from the corner. Hang it in the Louvre.

Marcos Coll, Colombia vs. USSR | 1962 World Cup

The most impressive part of the first Olimpico to be scored at a World Cup is who Coll beat in the USSR goal: the legendary Lev Yashin.

Megan Rapinoe, United States vs. Canada | 2012 London Olympics

When it comes to scoring an Olimpico at the Olympics, only one player in soccer history has managed the feat: USWNT icon Rapinoe.

Elise Kellond-Knight, Australia vs. Norway | 2019 Women's World Cup

The Matildas may have got knocked out of the 2019 Women's World Cup on penalties, but they'll always have Kellond-Knight's amazing Olimpico at the Allianz Riviera in Nice.

Leandro Carvalho, Ceará vs. Corinthians | 2019-20 Brazilian Serie A

Carvalho's Olimpico was cunning and spectacular, catching the defence sleeping and using the outside of his foot. What's more, it was scored in the 92nd minute to level the scores at 2-2 against São Paulo giants Corinthians.

Megan Rapinoe, United States vs. Australia | 2020 Tokyo Olympics

Remember when we said that Rapinoe was the only player in soccer history to score an Olimpico at the Olympic Games? Well she's did it twice, repeating her 2012 stunner over eight years later in Tokyo.

Hakan Çalhanoglu, Internazionale vs. AS Roma | 2020-21 Serie A

Why is Çalhanoglu's goal against AS Roma -- in Rome -- so memorable? It's an Olimpico at the Stadio Olimpico of course! How good.

Kyra Cooney-Cross, Melbourne Victory vs. Sydney FC | 2020-21 A-League Women

In the 120th minute of the A-League Women Grand Final, 19-year-old Cooney-Cross stepped up to take a corner ... and wrote her name into Australian football folklore.

Katie Zelem, Manchester United vs. Leicester City | 2021-22 Women's Super League

Scoring one Olimpico is hard enough, but Zelem managed to do it twice in one game. What's more, Zelem scored an Olimpico in the match before this one too.

Katie McCabe, Republic of Ireland vs. Canada | 2023 Women's World Cup

In their first appearance at a Women's World Cup, captain McCabe made sure Ireland fans would never forget the tournament with this inspirational strike.

Christian Pulisic, AC Milan vs. Club Brugge | 2024-25 UEFA Champions League

USMNT star Pulisic called it "a bit of luck" at the time, but there's no doubting the quality of his strike for AC Milan in their 3-1 win over Club Brugge in last season's Champions League league phase.

Son Heung-Min, Tottenham Hotspur vs. Manchester United | 2024-25 Carabao Cup

No Olimpico list would be complete without Son's stunner that sent Manchester United packing in the 2024-25 Carabao Cup quarterfinals. The South Korea skipper's crazy 88th-minute strike was the perfect denouement of a topsy-turvy match that finished 4-3 after Spurs had been leading 3-0.

Ángel Di María, Rosario Central vs. Boca Juniors | 2025 Liga Profesional de Fútbol

Last, but certainly not least, is this beauty from Di María for Rosario Central in their 1-1 draw with Boca Juniors in September. The Argentina star has a habit of scoring from corners, with this one -- astonishingly -- his fourth Olimpico.

stories.headline: Tom Brady tops list of athletes who became owners
stories.summary: The legendary quarterback is a member of an exclusive list of athletes that includes LeBron James, Serena Williams and Wayne Gretzky.
stories.body:
Tom Brady is getting (back) into the ownership game.

On Friday, sources confirmed to ESPN and NFL Network that the former superstar quarterback had bought shares in the English soccer giants Chelsea. Brady's purchasing of Chelsea shares comes after he departed the ownership group of another English club, EFL Championship side Birmingham City, earlier in the month after originally becoming a minority owner with a 3.3% stake.

Brady's latest interest isn't his only foray into the world of ownership -- he also owns a 5% minority stake in the Las Vegas Raiders, purchased in 2024, and he also has a stake in the Las Vegas Aces.

The NFL legend is far from the first athlete, active or former, to enter the ownership sphere. Here are other athletes who are now team owners:

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Atlético Madrid

In October 26 news broke that the star Oklahoma City Thunder guard would be joining the club as an investor.

"I am excited to officially join the group of shareholders of Atlético de Madrid," Gilgeous-Alexander said in the club's post. "This is a club with a long history at the top of European football, and I am grateful for the opportunity to be part of its future."

Jason Kidd -- Everton

In April 2025, English Premier League club Everton announced that then-Dallas Mavericks coach Jason Kidd would be adding a different title to his résumé: ownership group member. The news came after Kidd joined Roundhouse Capital Holdings, which is part of the Friedkin Group -- the U.S. firm that completed its takeover of Everton's ownership the previous December.

Vince Carter, Tracy McGrady, Jozy Altidore -- Buffalo Bills

In December 2024, the Bills announced Carter, McGrady and Altidore were among 10 limited partners the team was adding to its ownership group. Both McGrady (New York Knicks) and Altidore (New York Red Bulls) played for New York-area teams, while Carter spent time with the Brooklyn Nets (who were known as the New Jersey Nets at the time) and was McGrady's teammate on the Toronto Raptors (who are closer to Buffalo than NYC-based teams).

Tom Brady -- Las Vegas Aces, Las Vegas Raiders, Chelsea

The Las Vegas Aces, the reigning WNBA champions, have added to their championship credentials. Seven-time Super Bowl champion Tom Brady acquired a minority stake in the team whose majority owner is Las Vegas Raiders owner Mark Davis.

"I have always been a huge fan of women's sports, and I admire the work that the Aces' players, staff, and the WNBA continue to do to grow the sport and empower future generations of athletes," Brady said in a statement. "To be able to contribute in any way to that mission as a member of the Aces organization is an incredible honor."

Brady attended an Aces game in May 2022 and sent gifts to star Kelsey Plum. Plum and other Aces players were excited to have Brady as part of the team.

He also added the Las Vegas Raiders to his resume after his purchase of minority stake in the franchise was approved by NFL teams owners on Tuesday. The deal was agreed on in May 2023, but it took owners 17 months to give their approval over concerns he was receiving too much of a discount from majority owner Mark Davis.

Brady was also a minority owner of Birmingham City, a club in English soccer's second-tier Championship, but sold his shares in November 2026. He purchased shares in Chelsea later that month.

Lewis Hamilton -- Denver Broncos

The Broncos' ownership group added racing royalty in August 2022. Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton has a stake with the Walton-Penner group, which purchased the team in June 2022.

Hamilton, 37, has the Formula One record for most race wins and has won the Formula One title seven times. The ownership group, which purchased the team for $4.65 billion, is led by Walmart heir Rob Walton and includes former U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, who also has a stake.

In April, Hamilton joined with Serena Williams in a consortium led by former Liverpool chairman Martin Broughton in an attempt to buy Premier League club Chelsea.

"He is a champion competitor who knows what it takes to lead a winning team," Walton said in a statement.

Marshawn Lynch -- Seattle Kraken

Lynch spent 13 seasons in Seattle with the Seahawks, but his new sports venture in the state of Washington is on the ice. On April 18, he joined the Seattle Kraken ownership team as a minority investor. The former NFL running back will be a part of the NHL's "Hockey is for Everyone" campaign and Kraken owner Tod Leiweke said Lynch expressed interest in shadowing him to learn hockey CEO operations.

"This is something I never would have imagined," Lynch said to CNBC in a statement. "I always dreamed of playing on a professional team but owning one is something special. As I look back on some of my accomplishments...I'm [going to] continue to count my blessings."

Grammy Award-winning artist and Seattle native Macklemore also joined the Kraken ownership team with Lynch.

Wayne Gretzky, Steve Nash and Dustin Johnson -- Las Vegas Desert Dogs

Wayne Gretzky is a big lacrosse guy? Yep, you read that right. The Great One may have made his name on the ice, but before Gretzky was the pride of the Edmonton Oilers he was a bona fide lax bro.

"The national sport of Canada is box lacrosse," Gretzky said. "I started playing lacrosse on a team at the age of six and played all the way until I was 16 years old. I have a great love for the game in the sense I really think that box lacrosse was such a crucial part of the success I ultimately had in ice hockey."

Because of this, it shouldn't be completely surprising that the hockey legend is linking up with 2020 Masters champion Dustin Johnson, NBA Hall of Famer and current Brooklyn Nets head coach Steve Nash and Nets owner Joe Tsai as part of a star-studded ownership group for the National Lacrosse League's newest expansion team in Las Vegas, the Desert Dogs.

Dwyane Wade -- Utah Jazz

Seeing Dwyane Wade support any team other than the Miami Heat is decidedly jarring. In April, the three-time NBA champion purchased an ownership stake in the Utah Jazz, joining majority owner and team governor Ryan Smith, and expressed a desire to take an active role in the franchise. D. Wade made good on his promise. He could be seen courtside throughout the season; he took action when an unsettling fan incident went down during the postseason, and he became a mentor to then-Jazz star Donovan Mitchell.

The former Miami Heat star also added to his portfolio with something a bit closer to home. Wade, a Chicago native, joined the ownership group of the WNBA's Chicago Sky.

"It's a great opportunity to be a part of the league in its very early stages. ... Growth is going to happen, and so I want to be a part of the growth of this league," Wade said.

Kevin Durant -- Philadelphia Union, NJ/NY Gotham FC

In June 2020, Brooklyn Nets star Kevin Durant purchased a 5% stake in MLS' Philadelphia Union, and he has an option to purchase an additional 5% at a later date. Durant also had engaged in talks about purchasing part of D.C. United the year prior, but he said the discussion never progressed.

Durant expanded his portfolio in May of this year, after being named as a minority owner of the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) club NJ/NY Gotham FC.

Thirty Five Ventures (35V), a company co-founded by the two-time NBA champion and entrepreneur Rich Kleiman, made a significant investment to acquire a stake in the club, marking the company's second investment in a professional soccer team.

Renee Montgomery -- Atlanta Dream

Former Atlanta Dream guard Renee Montgomery made history in February as part of a three-member investor group that was approved to purchase the team. Montgomery is the first former player to become both an owner and executive of a WNBA franchise. The ownership change followed pressure on former Republican Sen. Kelly Loeffler to sell her share of the Dream, after she angered WNBA players with her opposition to the league's racial justice initiatives.

Patrick Mahomes -- Kansas City Royals

Patrick Mahomes is no stranger to winning. While the Kansas City Royals can't exactly say the same, you can't rule out that the quarterback's winning ways might rub off on the franchise now that he is part of their ownership group. If Mahomes' status as an icon in Kansas City was in question (it wasn't), this move surely cemented it. Becoming a baseball owner made sense on several levels for the Chiefs' QB1. Not only was Mahomes -- who played baseball in college -- a legitimate pro prospect, his father, Pat Mahomes, spent 11 seasons in Major League Baseball. He also had to find some way to put that $503 million contract extension to good use.

Venus and Serena Williams -- Miami Dolphins, Angel City FC

Winning major titles and making history, that's what the Williams sisters do. In 2009, Venus and Serena became the first Black female minority owners in the NFL by purchasing a part of the Miami Dolphins. Musicians Jimmy Buffett, Gloria and Emilio Estefan, Fergie and Marc Anthony also bought shares in the team -- the Dolphins' ownership group is nothing if not eclectic. Then, last year, Serena Williams became part of the star-studded Angel City FC ownership group bringing a NWSL team to Los Angeles in 2022.

Mia Hamm, Abby Wambach and Julie Foudy -- Angel City FC

When Angel City FC arrived on the scene it did so in style. Before we even knew the Los Angeles based NWSL club's name, we knew it had superstar backing like no other. Among the 14 former USWNT players who are part of the group are Mia Hamm, Abby Wambach and Julie Foudy. I would have named Lauren Holiday, Shannon Boxx, Rachel Buehler, Amanda Cromwell, Joy Fawcett, Tisha Venturini Hoch, Angela Hucles, Shannon MacMillan, Saskia Webber and sisters Lorrie Fair Allen and Ronnie Fair Sullins, but I was really trying to stay true to my whole "I'm only going to name 20 athletes" thing from the intro. There are also a bunch of celebrities in the mix, but we don't have that kind of time.

Michael Jordan -- Charlotte Hornets

While we're on the subject of owners who haven't had the type of success we grew accustomed to in their playing days, I would be remiss if I didn't mention the GOAT. In 2010, Michael Jordan became the first ex-player to be a majority owner in the league when the NBA's Board of Governors unanimously approved his $275 million bid to buy the then Charlotte Bobcats in his home state of North Carolina. After a decade of underwhelming years, things look to be on the up for the now Hornets with Rookie of the Year LaMelo Ball providing a long-awaited spark in the organization. Never forget when his dad said he could beat MJ one-on-one ... good times.

Alex Rodriguez -- Minnesota Timberwolves, Minnesota Lynx

I don't know what part of this purchase feels less ideal to me, that Alex Rodriguez and his 50-50 business partner Marc Lore are only pursuing acquiring the Minnesota Timberwolves and Lynx after their original plan to buy the New York Mets failed or that Timberwolves star Anthony Edwards had no idea who former MLB star A-Rod was. Either way, the $1.5 billion deal is expected to close around July 1.

David Beckham -- Inter Miami

David Beckham, iconic soccer player and remains-to-be-seen owner. Beckham -- who is incredibly hands on with the franchise -- is part of an ownership group which was initially called Miami Beckham United but now operates under the name Miami Freedom Park LLC. Beckham and Inter Miami have seemingly been riddled with controversy since the club's inception in 2018. But all those problems could be a thing of the past if Lionel Messi decides to head to MLS. Hey, stranger things have happened.

LeBron James -- Liverpool

Back in 2011, LeBron James and manager Maverick Carter became minority owners of Premier League club Liverpool after Fenway Sports Group, which purchased the team in 2010, became the sole marketer of James' global rights. The deal has turned out to be pretty lucrative for James -- his original stake in the club, valued at about $6.5 million, had grown to about $32 million as of 2018. In 2019, Liverpool won the Premier League for their first top-flight league title in thirty years.

James Harden -- Houston Dynamo, Houston Dash

James Harden might not be in Houston anymore, but the former Rockets superstar's presence is still felt in the city. The Beard purchased a 5% stake in the group that controls MLS' Houston Dynamo and NWSL's Houston Dash in 2019. Boxer Oscar De La Hoya is also part of the group. The Dash won their first NWSL title last year, so he's probably feeling pretty good about that investment.

Russell Wilson and Ken Griffey Jr. -- Seattle Sounders

What do Russell Wilson, Ken Griffey Jr. and Macklemore have in common? They are all part of the Seattle Sounders' ownership group. Wilson, along with his wife, musician Ciara, purchased a stake in the team in 2019 -- just in time for them to win an MLS Cup title. Griffey Jr. and his family followed suit in November 2020.

Zlatan Ibrahimovic -- Hammaraby

Seemingly everything Zlatan does makes people react intensely, and that remained true when he purchased part of Swedish team Hammaraby back in 2019. Fans of Malmo, another Swedish team where Zlatan started his professional career, reacted by vandalizing a statue of Zlatan outside the team's home stadium, placing a toilet seat around one of its arms.

Magic Johnson -- Los Angeles Dodgers

Big LA guy. In 2012, Lakers great Magic Johnson was part of a group that bought the Los Angeles Dodgers from Frank McCourt for a record $2 billion. At the time, the price shattered the mark for a sports franchise. Magic kept it real at the time of purchase when explaining his role in recruiting free agents, saying that while he can't talk hitting or pitching with players, he "can talk winning." If recent history is any indication (in case you blacked out all of 2020 -- the Dodgers won the World Series), it worked.

stories.headline: Kangaroos bounce Kiwis for fourth-straight Rugby League World Cup title
stories.summary: The Kangaroos have won a fourth-straight Rugby League World Cup, toppling New Zealand 32-12 in Brisbane.
stories.body:
The Kangaroos have punished a disappointing New Zealand, with Reece Walsh running riot in a 32-12 World Cup final waltz.

There was an expectation the Kiwis, searching for their second Cup title and first since 2008, would push Australia all the way after a two-point loss in a pulsating tournament opener.

But the visitors struggled from the outset in Brisbane on Sunday night, Jamayne Isaako's kick-off floating long in a sign of things to come.

Walsh dazzled at fullback for the Kangaroos, his pace, vision and wicked footwork too much as he helped lay on two tries and generally wreak havoc around the ruck and close to the line.

Conversely, Walsh's New Zealand opposite Kalyn Ponga -- International Rugby League's Golden Boot winner on Thursday night -- was unable to get into game.

Australian hooker Harry Grant and halves Tom Dearden and Cam Munster completely outplayed their error-riddled opposites, while the Kangaroos' pack muscled up.

Dearden laid on two first-half tries for Liam Martin with well-timed short balls, while Bradman Best was rewarded for an inspired chase-down tackle of Jahrome Hughes with a try soon after.

When Tom Trbojevic scored to begin the second half it was 28-6 and effectively game over.

Jack Bostock completed his breakout season with a try in each half for Australia.

It was the Kangaroos' fourth consecutive title and 10th in the last 11 tournaments, dating back to 1975.

stories.headline: Making sense of the Jaguars going for two, then kicking a field goal down eight
stories.summary: The Jaguars made it 23-15 late vs. the Giants, but their two-point try failed. They got the ball back ... but kicked a field goal, leaving them down 23-18?
stories.body:
The Jaguars made two controversial game management decisions in the fourth quarter of their 23-18 loss to the Giants on Sunday -- going for two down eight points with 6:39 left and then attempting a field goal down eight with 3:40 left.

Did they make the right calls? According to ESPN Analytics, the first was a no-brainer ... and the second was a knife's edge decision in which either choice would have been acceptable.

Let's break them both down and make some sense of what happened.

Decision No. 1: Attempting a two-point conversion down 23-15 with 6:39 left following Brian Thomas Jr.'s touchdown catch
This is a standard "down eight, go for two" scenario. We've written about it at length in the past, but the abridged version is that this sets the Jaguars up for a better situation after their next touchdown as they try to come back. If they convert the two-point attempt, then they can kick a PAT to take the lead on the next touchdown. If they fail the two-point attempt, then they can go for two and still have a chance to tie on the next touchdown.

In this case, the Jaguars increased their chance to win the game by 1.4 percentage points by going for two. They needed just a 35% chance of conversion to justify going for two, and the league average is 48%.

Of course, the Jaguars failed to convert the two-point attempt, but that doesn't change our evaluation of their decision. Kicking the PAT would have been a clear-as-day error.

Decision No. 2: Attempting a field goal on fourth-and-goal at the Giants' 8-yard line still down 23-15 with 3:40 left
ESPN Analytics' model had both options -- kicking the field goal or going for it -- as yielding almost identical win probabilities for the Jaguars at that point: 13.7% either way. In other words, either choice was reasonable.

This will likely catch many people off guard; I'm sure most people figure the Jaguars should have gone for it down one score late in the fourth quarter. Had the Jaguars gone for it, they would have needed to convert (our model estimates a 32% chance) and then convert the ensuing two-point attempt to tie.

That last word is the key, and I think it's where the disconnect occurs. We can't equate taking the lead and tying the game, because they are very different. By kicking the field goal, the Jaguars were taking the risk that they might not get the ball back -- which is what happened. But by reducing the deficit to five points, they also gave themselves the chance to win the game with a touchdown if they did get the ball back.

That's not to say kicking was preferable. But it's the reason why it was about the same as going for it.

Were the decisions connected?
Yes. Had the Jaguars been down only seven points instead of eight (as would have been the case if Jacksonville had kicked the PAT), that would have changed the calculation on the fourth down. But ... had they been down only six points instead of eight (as would have been the case if Jacksonville had converted the two-point try), that also would have changed the calculation.

Does that mean they made a mistake by going for two earlier?
It does not. When we talk about going for two down eight, we simplify the scenario down to when the trailing team scores again and the leading team doesn't. But our model is not making those same simplifications in making its recommendation. And it comes back with the same conclusion: Going for two down eight late (starting around halfway through the third quarter) is virtually always worth it.

stories.headline: What Tarik Skubal's massive deal means for Mets, suitors, all of MLB
stories.summary: The two-time Cy Young winner is now baseball's highest paid pitcher ever. Here's how Skubal's contract impacts the league.
stories.body:
Tarik Skubal is officially headed to the New York Mets on a record-setting $450 million contract. Skubal pitched the final months of the 2026 MLB season with the Los Angeles Dodgers following a midseason blockbuster trade from Detroit, where he had previously spent his entire career. After a free agency that earned interest from plenty of contenders, the superstar ace decided on the Mets on Sunday, ending his stay in L.A.

His nine-year, $450 million contract is now the largest in major league history for a pitcher. How does it change New York's outlook for 2027 -- and beyond? Where should the Dodgers and other suitors turn now? And what does it mean for baseball ahead of the impending lockout?

Our MLB experts weigh in on Skubal's sport-altering deal.

What is your initial impression of Skubal's $450 million deal ahead of the expected lockout?
Buster Olney: The contract numbers landed around where many in baseball believed they would, and it's not a surprise that it came down to the Mets. They were desperate to sign him; owner Steve Cohen had negotiated a monster deal with Skubal's agent, Scott Boras, before; and Cohen is one of the few owners -- maybe the only one -- seemingly unconcerned with the potential financial ramifications for his team if baseball's financial system changes dramatically under a new collective bargaining agreement. It was as if Captain Cohen shouted, "Damn the salary cap torpedoes, full speed ahead!"

Skubal gets paid, a little more than a week before the lockout deadline. But it appears more and more likely that 200-plus free agents will go without deals before the next CBA is forged.

What does it mean for the Mets to get an ace for the next nine years?
Jorge Castillo: They finally have a true No. 1 starter. Nolan McLean has ace potential, and he might reach it next season after a promising rookie year, but the Mets under president of baseball operations David Stearns have not employed a proven top-shelf starting pitcher. That's largely because Stearns prefers not to give free agent starting pitchers long-term contracts. The only other long-term contract the Mets have offered to a free-agent starter under Stearns was Yoshinobu Yamamoto three years ago. But Yamamoto was 25. Skubal just turned 30. He has undergone three surgeries on his left elbow. This is not a Stearns move -- it's a Steve Cohen move, and it will bolster a rotation that has been a problem the past two seasons.

Alden Gonzalez: It means they have a tone-setter for their rotation, to go along with Juan Soto and Francisco Lindor as the faces of the position-player group. Skubal is arguably the best pitcher in the world -- and he's also someone McLean, Jonah Tong, Christian Scott and Jonathan Santucci can follow. David Stearns still has a lot of work to do with his roster, but he now has a foundation from which to build out the rest of his pitching staff.

What else can New York do to have a perfect offseason from here?
Bradford Doolittle: More. The Mets need more offense, more walks, better defense, more pitching. Of all that, getting a legit power-and-patience hitter at first base would be at the top of my list. Who? Maybe one of the overseas guys, Teruaki Sato (somewhat pricey to sign) or Koo Ja-wook (probably not expensive to sign). You can always juggle corner players, so you can't get too hung up on the first-base qualifier.

David Schoenfield: I'm with Brad on upgrading first base -- even though Jorge Polanco and Mark Vientos are still on the roster. If you want to believe in Ty France's 2026 resurgence, he's another possibility (and a good defender as well). He's risky given his age (32) and 2023-25 performance, but he did make some changes that helped him improve his exit velo and launch angle. Otherwise: bullpen. It wasn't terrible in 2026, but a quick scan of the roster doesn't exactly inspire confidence either. If money is no object -- and it apparently isn't -- Adrian Morejon is a must.

Where should Skubal's other suitors turn this offseason after missing out on the ace?

Gonzalez: The Los Angeles Dodgers wanted Skubal back, but they never got to the point of making an offer, according to sources. The potential of a salary cap and the general uncertainties of baseball's economic model with the collective bargaining agreement set to expire made them reluctant to make the type of long-term commitment it took to land him. The extent to which a federal investigation into Mark Walter's finances had an impact is unknown, though it has surely been heavily speculated upon. The Dodgers would still like to add a starting pitcher to address some of the volatility in a rotation fronted by Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani and Tyler Glasnow, three players whose workloads are always uncertain. They have Emmet Sheehan, Justin Wrobleski, Roki Sasaki and Gavin Stone behind them -- and Yamamoto, too, of course -- but look for them to add another starter regardless.

Castillo: Freddy Peralta fits the Toronto Blue Jays well for a few reasons. One is that his fastball would play up at Rogers Centre. We saw Peralta turn his season around upon getting traded to the Tampa Bay Rays at the deadline. That was partly, in addition to a few mechanical and pitch mix changes, because his fastball has more induced vertical break indoors, and the Rays call Tropicana Field, the only fixed-roof ballpark in the majors, home. "Fastball Freddy" combined that with an increase in velocity to salvage his platform season. Rogers Centre has a retractable roof. A lot of his starts would be inside. That matters. And it matters that the Blue Jays are willing to spend top dollar to further improve their rotation after giving Dylan Cease a seven-year, $210 million contract last winter.

Gonzalez: That the San Diego Padres were in on Skubal was an indication of how financially committed the new ownership group might be to bringing San Diego its first championship, but they were always better off spreading that money out to several pitchers. The Padres don't just need an ace -- they need several proven starters. At the moment, the only one in their rotation is Randy Vasquez, with Joe Musgrove and Yu Darvish both mysteries heading into 2027. So far this offseason, they've been in on practically everybody. And it would be a shock not to see them come away with multiple starting pitchers before the expected Dec. 1 lockout. The Padres need to address first base and left field, and ideally they'd also add to the back end of their bullpen, but starting pitching is by far their biggest priority. Look for them to get aggressive there now that Skubal is off the board.

What does this signing do to the 2027 playoff picture in both leagues?
Jesse Rogers: The balance of star power in MLB might have switched coasts but not leagues, as Skubal heading to the Mets keeps the National League an arms-length ahead of the American League heading into 2027. It also allows for some optimism in Queens, where New York hasn't been very productive on the mound lately. Now the NL East boasts aces in Skubal, Chris Sale (Atlanta Braves) and Cristopher Sanchez (Philadelphia Phillies), which should make for a good race in the division. That's assuming the Mets bounce back and Skubal gives them the boost they need.

On the other side of the NL, the Dodgers won't miss Skubal the way other teams might have if they'd lost him. They were good before he arrived. They're still good.

Doolittle: Probably not much in the AL. In the NL, the Mets leapfrog the Braves in the NL East, just behind Philadelphia, but all three are tightly bunched. And all three are way behind the Dodgers and remain well behind the Milwaukee Brewers. This signing does boost the Mets' playoff chances by 17%, up to around 59%. And that's just for year one. It's a major add.

stories.headline: Way-too-early look ahead to the 2027 AFL Draft: 15 players to know
stories.summary: The 2027 AFL Draft will look markedly different to the past few years with the introduction of Tasmania. Who are the players to know? Jasper Chellappah has named 15 to keep an eye on next year.
stories.body:
On to the next.

The 2027 AFL Draft will look markedly different to the past few years, with Tasmania's inclusion making for an expansion draft similar to that of 2010 and 2011. The Devils own picks 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, and 13 in the first round, plus the first pick of each subsequent round as part of concessions.

The club will need to trade 5, 7, 11, and 13 or roll them into 2028 or 2029. That means the competition's 19th team will take 1, 3 and 9 to the draft next year.

Tasmania has also pre-listed some of the brightest talents in the crop. Axel Walsh, Baxter Sruk, and Jake Miller were all clear pick No. 1 contenders 12 months out from their draft, and will attend school in Hobart and play football in the VFL next year.

Five Tasmania-tied teens have been included in the ones to watch next year. Another three are club-tied, making 2027 the most compromised draft in AFL history. Twenty-three of the 46 prospects in the AFL Futures exhibition on Grand Final day were club-tied.

Perhaps the saving grace for 18 other clubs is the fact that 2027 has been touted as an elite draft class for some time. There's premium talent still in the open pool and another 12 months for more quality to emerge, with a heavy leaning towards midfielders.

With an extended 15 prospects given the club-tied nature of the class, this is ESPN's way-too-early look ahead to the best prospects in the 2027 AFL Draft.

1. Axel Walsh (Tasmania pre-list)

East Perth/Western Australia

RUC, 201cm

Another in the resurgence of premium ruck prospects in the draft, and perhaps the best. Walsh is a monster in the air; his best traits come with his aerial strength where he drifts back to intercept mark, pushes forward to stretch defences and dominates around the ground. He will fill out to become a true ruck size and is as close to Max Gawn as a prospect has been this decade. Walsh would be the pick one favourite if he wasn't pre-listed by Tasmania.

2. Baxter Sruk (Tasmania pre-list)

Eastern Ranges/Vic Metro

MID, 185cm

Sruk has been a big game performer and consistent midfield standout in the Talent League. He's a physical on-baller that throws his weight around, impacts with his ball-winning and gets forward to kick goals in bunches. Sruk thrives in the heat of the contest and brings tenacity to Tasmania's list.

3. Jake Miller (Tasmania pre-list)

Western Jets/Vic Metro

FWD, 197cm

Miller is the leading key forward prospect next year. He enjoyed a stellar national championships as a bottom-ager, named to the All-Australian team as well as the Talent League All-Australian side. Miller is a brilliant mark with arms outstretched, able to take big contested marks in packs and secure the ball on long searching leads. He's a reliable set shot off his left foot and is an elite runner for his size. Tasmania has already pre-listed the immense talent.

4. Max Thompson

Bendigo Pioneers/Vic Country

FWD/MID, 175cm

Thompson has played in varying positions and looked good but is clearly at his best inside 50. He's smart and crafty, puts speed on the game and is a wonderfully fluid kick of the ball. Thompson can get up the ground and beat his man back to goals, distribute off halfback or win his own ball. He's the type of versatile small forward that clubs will covet.

5. James Artemis

East Fremantle/Western Australia

MID, 177cm

A leading contender in the open pool, Artemis is the cousin of Essendon's Jaxon and will have suitors very early in the draft. He's a hard-nosed contested midfielder that can then link up transition with hard running and slick ball use. He's dogged with the ball up for grabs and then powers through contact to get it moving forward.

6. Koby Bewick (Essendon father-son)

Calder Cannons/Vic Metro

MID, 178cm

Modern footy suits Bewick down to the ground. The son of 1993 and 2000 premiership small forward Darren, the Calder midfielder has been thrown around in different positions but has all the traits to become an excellent on-baller. He's incisive with his movement and foot skills on the outside, and possesses the running base and work ethic to rack up a lot of the ball in transition. He comes alive in open space where he can run and carry and pick out targets inside 50, which could see him start his career off halfback or a wing. Bewick kicked two goals from 19 touches in his Futures outing.

7. Zemes Pilot (Port Adelaide NGA)

South Adelaide/South Australia

FWD/MID, 193cm

Pilot is an elite basketball talent as well, so it's a coup for footy that the 193cm forward is opting to pursue opportunities in Port's NGA. The uber-athletic tall forward is incredible to watch, soaring above packs to take epic marks, breaking ankles with sharp agility and kicking goals from ridiculous angles. He had a game last year in the SANFL U16s with 27 disposals and 9.4 in front of goals.

8. Jett Flower

Eastern Ranges/Vic Metro

MID/DEF, 183cm

Flower is the grandson of Melbourne legend Robbie, and one of the top open pool prospects in 2027. Boasting one of the best names to come through the pathways in some time, Flower is a classy outside midfielder with beautiful foot skills and a strong running base. He likely appeals to clubs as a rebounder out of defence with his competitiveness a feature behind the ball. Flower was best afield in the Futures game with 17 disposals and a goal.

9. Louis Salopek (Port Adelaide father-son)

Dandenong Stingrays/Vic Country

MID/FWD, 186cm

A genuine star of the crop, Salopek has been in the wars across the past year or so, enduring three separate incidents of a collapsed lung. He burst onto the scene for Vic Country in the U16s champs and plays with a high motor, tackling and pressuring through the midfield and pushing forward to hit the scoreboard. He's keen to get to the Power as the son of Steven.

10. Riley Stratford (Tasmania pre-list)

Sandringham Dragons/Vic Metro

MID, 188cm

A taller midfielder who still needs to build into his frame, Stratford has been part of some massive games in his junior career. He was a star for Brighton Grammar on the way to an inaugural APS title and can play on a wing or through the engine room with impact in the air. Tasmania has locked him away and he'll play for their VFL side next year.

11. Oscar Henwood

Gippsland Power/Vic Country

MID, 185cm

Henwood was a key contributor in the Power's Talent League flag and plays with great composure. He can try to bite off too much with his time in possession but is typically creative and uses it really well in space.

12. Harvey Chapman

Sturt/South Australia

DEF, 195cm

Chapman is the lone key defender inside the top bracket of the draft 12 months out, though he plays a more natural role as a rebounder. The SA tall is an excellent kick and sets up play from the last line of defence with instructive ball use. He can intercept with his reading of the play and gets involved in attack up the field.

13. Sam Husband (Tasmania Academy)

Tasmania Devils/Allies

MID, 180cm

The Devils didn't pre-list Husband because they have priority access to Tasmanian in the draft. He's the premier Tassie prospect in their inaugural draft and will be the poster boy of local talent for the 19th team. He's already played two seasons of Talent League football and is at his best using his evasiveness and skills around stoppages.

14. Campbell Creyk

West Perth/Western Australia

MID, 182cm

Creyk surged into the first round mix this year as a contested beast through the midfield. He rips the ball out of stoppages and doesn't often lose one-on-ones, playing with a hard edge that will serve him well at the next level. He will need to round out his game on the outside to continue pushing up draft boards.

15. Taj Garrett

Sturt/South Australia

MID, 183cm

A hard-running midfielder, Garrett's thirst to find the ball and work to contests is an important facet of his game. He outworks opponents and gets forward of the ball to impact. He may play his best football off a wing in the AFL but will get ample exposure on-ball for Sturt next year.

stories.headline: Reports: Dynamo's Herrera charged with DWI, club aware of 'incident'
stories.summary: Houston Dynamo FC midfielder Héctor Herrera was charged with driving while intoxicated on Saturday in Montgomery County, Texas, according to multiple reports.
stories.body:
Houston Dynamo FC midfielder Héctor Herrera was charged with driving while intoxicated on Saturday in Montgomery County, Texas, according to multiple reports.

MLS and the Houston Dynamo said in a statement to ESPN on Sunday that they are looking into an "incident" involving Herrera.

"The Houston Dynamo are aware of an incident involving Héctor Herrera on Friday night. The Club and Major League Soccer are working to gather additional information," said the Dynamo's statement to ESPN. "We will refrain from providing further comment until appropriate."

The Dynamo are set to begin a best-of-three playoff series against the San Jose Earthquakes on Nov. 24. It is unclear whether Herrera will be available for the match.

The situation could mark another misstep for Herrera, who was sent off in 2024 for spitting on a referee. Following the event, the Dynamo denied his 2025 contract extension, before bringing him back for the 2026 season.

Between 2022 to 2024, Herrera made 69 appearances (including playoffs) for the Dynamo. The Pachuca academy product then made his way to Liga MX's Toluca in 2025, where he won the Clausura and Apertura titles in Mexico's top-flight.

Since his return to Houston in 2026, Herrera has made 30 appearances across the regular season. The midfielder has three goals and two assists this year.

Spotrac's Caleb Pongratz was the first to report the news and the Houston Chronicle published a story Sunday with confirmation of the charge from the Montgomery County sheriff's office.

stories.headline: Bruno Fernandes disputes Leny Yoro red card in Liverpool's rout of Man United
stories.summary: Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes was not happy with the officiating in Sunday's 4-0 drubbing at Liverpool.
stories.body:
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes was not happy with the officiating in Sunday's 4-0 drubbing at Liverpool, insisting Leny Yoro's early challenge on Alexander Isak was "never a red card."

Yoro was dismissed in the eighth minute by referee Sam Barrott for what was deemed a last-man foul that denied Isak a goalscoring opportunity following Matthijs de Ligt's mistake, with Dominik Szoboszlai scoring from the resulting free-kick.

The Reds went on to complete a comprehensive rout over the 10 men with further goals from Florian Wirtz, Rio Ngumoha and Víctor Muñoz as Mauricio Pochettino's Red Devils reign got off to a miserable start at Anfield.

The new head coach said he took full ownership of the result but felt the Yoro sending off changed the course of the game, with his skipper in agreement and feeling the wrong decision had been reached.

The Portugal midfielder told BBC Sport: "I can understand the fall, but it's never a red card.

"I think it's too many referees on the pitch and too many on VAR, seated, with such a long time to see and put it back, go forward, put it back, do it in slow motion, whatsoever.

"To make a mistake like this can change a game. But obviously, then, it's not because of them that we concede the goal from the free-kick, but it changes completely the flow of the game."
